kurz: Why the US has no saver's allowance but lets many households realize long-term gains at 0%, how tax-gain harvesting works, and which accounts shelter investment income altogether.

bloecke.md:
The federal income tax has no separate allowance for investment income. Instead, three mechanisms keep investment income tax-free in practice. The first is the standard deduction, which applies to all income including interest and dividends. For 2026 it is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly. The second is the 0% rate on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, which applies up to $49,450 of taxable income for single filers and $98,900 for joint filers in 2026. The third, and for most savers the most important, is the set of tax-advantaged accounts such as the 401(k), the IRA and the HSA.

Interest and short-term gains have no special exemption beyond the standard deduction; they are taxed at ordinary rates from the first dollar of taxable income. Investment expenses are not deductible either. With $3,000 of interest and $400 of custody or advisory fees, $3,000 counts as income.

bloecke.titel: No form needed, but a return
bloecke.md: The 0% rate is not something you apply for at the bank. Nothing is withheld on investment income anyway, and the rate is applied automatically when you file Form 1040. That also means it only helps if you file. A return showing $0 tax can still be required, for example because your gross income exceeds the filing threshold.

## How the 0% range is used up

Long-term gains and qualified dividends are stacked on top of ordinary taxable income. Your wages, interest and short-term gains, minus the standard deduction, fill the brackets first. Only the remaining room up to the 0% threshold is available for preferential income at 0%.

A single person with no other income can therefore receive $16,100 + $49,450 = $65,550 of long-term gains and qualified dividends in 2026 without owing any federal income tax. For a married couple filing jointly, it is $32,200 + $98,900 = $131,100. Retirees who live on savings and early retirees often fall into this range, and so do students and households with low wage income in a given year.

bloecke.formel: Room at 0% = 0% threshold − (Ordinary income − Standard deduction)
bloecke.erklaerung: If ordinary income is lower than the standard deduction, the unused deduction also offsets preferential income, and the room grows by that amount. The result can never be negative; if it is, all preferential income is taxed at 15% or more.
variablen: wages, interest, short-term gains, nonqualified dividends, IRA withdrawals
bloecke.beispiel: A married couple with $90,000 of wages has $57,800 of ordinary taxable income. They can realize $41,100 of long-term gains at 0%.

bloecke.titel: Long-term gains that fit into the 0% range (married filing jointly, 2026)
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the 2026 standard deduction of $32,200 and a 0% threshold of $98,900, assuming wages are the only other income. Above about $131,000 of wages, no room is left.

bloecke.md: The 2026 amounts come from the IRS inflation adjustments for 2026 and the 2025 budget law, which raised the standard deduction. Taxpayers aged 65 or older receive an additional standard deduction, and for 2025 to 2028 a further deduction of up to $6,000 per person, which phases out at higher incomes. Both increase the room at 0%. The NIIT does not matter here, because its thresholds of $200,000 and $250,000 lie far above the 0% range. State income tax is a different matter: most states tax capital gains like other income and have no 0% rate, so a gain that is federally tax-free can still cost state tax.

## Tax-gain harvesting

If you have room at 0%, you can sell appreciated shares held for more than one year and buy them back immediately. The gain is taxed at 0%, and your basis rises to the current price. Unlike for losses, there is no waiting period: the wash sale rule only disallows losses, not gains. Economically nothing changes, but the gain realized today will not be taxed again later. The tax is not deferred but avoided, as long as the position is eventually sold at a gain.

Three points need care. Only long-term lots qualify, because short-term gains are ordinary income. Capital gains increase your adjusted gross income, which can reduce income-based benefits such as premium tax credits for marketplace health insurance, raise the taxable part of Social Security benefits and, two years later, increase Medicare premiums through IRMAA. And trading costs, while usually small, still apply through the bid-ask spread.

A married couple has $100,000 of wages. After the $32,200 standard deduction, their ordinary taxable income is $67,800, which leaves 98,900 − 67,800 = $31,100 of room at 0%. Their funds already pay $3,000 of qualified dividends this year, so $28,100 is left for gains.

Their index fund position has a gain of 40% of its value. To realize $28,100 of gain, they sell 28,100 ÷ 0.40 = $70,250 of shares and buy them back the same day.

At a later sale at 15%, this gain would have cost 28,100 × 15% = $4,215 of federal tax. In a state with a 5% income tax, the harvest costs $1,405 of state tax now, but that tax would have been due at a later sale anyway.

If you forget the dividends in the calculation, you realize $3,000 too much gain, and that part is taxed at 15%.

## Tax-advantaged accounts

The main US counterpart to a tax-free allowance is not a deduction but the account in which the investments are held. Inside a 401(k), 403(b), IRA, HSA or 529 plan, dividends, interest and gains are not taxed when they arise. No Form 1099-DIV or 1099-B is issued for them, and trading inside the account has no tax consequences.

The accounts differ in when tax is paid. With a traditional 401(k) or IRA, contributions are deducted or excluded now, and withdrawals are ordinary income later, including the gains, which lose their preferential rate. With a Roth 401(k) or Roth IRA, contributions are made from taxed income, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The HSA can be tax-free on both ends if the money is used for medical expenses. The annual limits cap how much can be sheltered.

bloecke.titel: $7,500 a year in a Roth IRA or in a taxable account
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: 7% total return a year, of which 1.5% are qualified dividends taxed at 15% each year in the taxable account; values after paying 15% on the remaining gain at the end. Contributions are made at the end of each year.

bloecke.md:
## Spouses and children

For married couples filing jointly, the standard deduction and the 0% threshold are exactly twice the single amounts. It makes no difference which spouse owns the shares. Filing separately rarely helps, because most thresholds are then halved.

Children are separate taxpayers, but the kiddie tax limits shifting investment income to them. It applies to children under 18, and in many cases to those under 19 or full-time students under 24. In 2025, the first $1,350 of a child's unearned income was tax-free, the next $1,350 was taxed at the child's rate, and anything above $2,700 at the parents' rate. Gifts to a child, typically through a custodial UTMA or UGMA account, are irrevocable: the money belongs to the child, who gains control at the age of majority set by state law, usually 18 or 21.

bloecke.md: A 529 plan owned by a parent counts as a parental asset for federal financial aid, which is weighted less heavily than assets owned by the student. That is one reason why many families save for education in a 529 plan rather than in a custodial account. Rules for using 529 money for other purposes, including limited rollovers to a Roth IRA, have their own conditions.

- Assuming that 0% tax means no return is needed. The gains still appear on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
- Harvesting a short-term gain. It is ordinary income and taxed at 10% or more.
- Forgetting that dividends and fund distributions use up the 0% range before the planned sale.
- Ignoring the side effects of a higher adjusted gross income on health insurance subsidies, Social Security taxation or Medicare premiums.
- Forgetting state income tax, which usually has no 0% rate.
- Contributing more than the annual limit to an IRA. The excess is subject to a 6% excise tax for every year it stays in the account.

mitnehmen: The US has no saver's allowance; instead, the standard deduction and the 0% rate on long-term gains and qualified dividends keep investment income tax-free up to $65,550 (single) or $131,100 (joint) in 2026 if there is no other income.
The 0% range is what is left after ordinary income has filled the brackets; dividends and fund distributions use it up first.
Tax-gain harvesting realizes long-term gains at 0% and raises the basis; the wash sale rule does not apply to gains, so you can buy back immediately.
Tax-advantaged accounts such as the 401(k), IRA and HSA are the main shelter: income inside them is not taxed while it stays invested.
Shifting income to children is limited by the kiddie tax, and custodial accounts are irrevocable gifts that the child controls at the age of majority.

begriffe.text: Fixed amount subtracted from adjusted gross income if you do not itemize: $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly in 2026. It reduces taxable income of every kind, including interest and dividends.
Part of taxable income up to $49,450 (single) or $98,900 (joint) in 2026 within which long-term gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%. Ordinary income fills it first.
Selling long-term positions with a gain while the gain falls into the 0% range and buying them back at once. It raises the basis without federal tax; the wash sale rule does not apply to gains.

Rule under which a child's unearned income above a threshold ($2,700 in 2025) is taxed at the parents' marginal rate (26 U.S.C. § 1(g)). It applies to children under 18 and, in many cases, to those under 19 or students under 24.
